name: カリーライス専門店エチオピア 本店 (Curry Rice Specialist Ethiopia (Honten / Mai)

claims.text: Official site carries a per-menu allergen chart listing wheat and soybeans as allergens present: 'ALL MENU such as shrimp, wheat, eggs, dairy, cashew nut, beef, soybeans, chicken, banana, pork, yam, lamb, apple, gelatin, sesame, are all displays as follows' — confirming wheat IS present somewhere in the menu, so a wheat-flour-free roux does not equal gluten-free.
claims.source: https://www.ethiopia-curry.com/ (allergen chart, quoted via search snippet)

claims.text: Cooking process confirmed as vegetable-spice paste simmered with meat extract over ~3 days ('肉のエキスでじっくり煮込み'), and this base underlies the vegetable curry and bean curry — confirms vegan 'no' and shows the base is a stock-based sauce that may also carry soy-sauce-derived wheat.

General Japanese curry allergen guidance: soybean listing in a curry base commonly reflects soy sauce or Worcestershire sauce used as a hidden seasoning; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat and is not gluten-free — a real, unmeasured gluten vector here.
The curry roux is made without wheat flour, thickened naturally from a long-simmered puree of celery, onion, and other vegetables with 12 spices rather than a store-bought roux.

The restaurant fries all tempura — shrimp, fish, and vegetable/kakiage items — in a shared sesame-oil fryer at a single tempura station; no allergen-segregated or dedicated gluten-free fryer is documented.
The signature tsuyu dipping sauce is described as a dark, concentrated, soy-sauce-based sauce; standard Japanese shoyu contains wheat and no wheat-free (tamari) alternative is mentioned.
Vegetable tempura/kakiage is fried in the same oil and at the same station as shrimp and other seafood tempura, so cross-contact with shellfish is likely for any vegetable items ordered.

name: 黄金の塩らぁ麺 ドゥエ イタリアン 東急プラザ渋谷店 (Due Italian – Tokyu Plaza Shibuya (Ougon no )

claims.text: The shop's 'healthy noodle' is marketed with gluten-free language but is actually a half wheat-flour / half konjac-noodle blend, meaning it still contains gluten and is unsafe for celiac diners despite the framing.
The 醤油らぁ麺 (soy-sauce ramen) is made with conventional shoyu, which is wheat-based.

The signature golden broth is built from chicken bones (鶏ガラ) simmered with kelp and scallop, and dishes are finished with cream cheese, Gorgonzola, and prosciutto — there is no vegan or vegetarian broth option.
A noodle-swap option (part-konjac) is available for those wanting a lower-carbohydrate bowl, though it is not a genuine gluten-free option.

The kitchen is described as excluding all animal-derived ingredients as well as the Buddhist "five pungent roots" (onion, garlic, chives, leek, scallion), consistent with strict shōjin-style plant-based cooking.
Menu and site descriptions consistently state the food uses no animal products at all (fully vegan shōjin ryori), not just a vegetarian subset of dishes.
A reviewer noted the noodle-dish broth was vegetable-only yet tasted deeply umami, suggesting deliberate care in building flavor without fish-based dashi.

name: ファラフェルブラザーズ 渋谷パルコ店 (Falafel Brothers Shibuya PARCO)

claims.text: Celiac review states it is 'not recommended for celiacs,' that you must be 'very, very explicit about cross contamination,' the food preparer 'didn't know anything about Celiac disease,' and cross-contamination is 'highly likely' — there is a lot of bread and no separate prep area, with hands filling pita bread and then going into the same bowl of salad used to make the rice plates.
Listing states this establishment is NOT a dedicated gluten-free facility and may not be safe for those with celiac disease.
Shop and aggregator listings market 'gluten-free menu' items and GF/sugar-free vegan sweets but publish no cross-contamination, shared-fryer, or allergen-protocol information.

The entire menu is plant-based/vegan (no meat, fish, dairy, or eggs), and the brand is described as using organic ingredients and being kosher-certified, reducing risk of hidden animal-derived ingredients such as dashi or bonito for vegan diners.
The falafel is chickpea-based with no wheat-flour binder, and the rice-plate menu option is noted as popular among gluten-free diners.

name: 魚山亭 渋谷店 (Gyossantei Shibuya)

claims.text: The restaurant's signature chicken nanban is deep-fried in a wheat-flour batter; no dedicated gluten-free fryer or allergy-accommodation policy was found in any source.

The specialty cold soup hiyajiru (冷や汁) is a miso-based dish traditionally made with dashi stock (commonly bonito-based) in Miyazaki-style preparations; no vegan-specific menu or substitution was found.

name: haishop cafe 渋谷スクランブルスクエア店 (haishop cafe Shibuya Scramble Square)

claims.text: Shop press release confirms only ~80% of the menu is vegan/vegetarian, meaning it is NOT a fully vegan kitchen and ~20% of items are non-vegan — individual vegan items must be verified.

HappyCow listing for Haishop Cafe is a general vegan/vegetarian directory entry; it surfaces no celiac rating, no gluten-free tag, and no cross-contamination review — i.e., no celiac-grade corroboration exists.
FindMeGlutenFree Shibuya City celiac/gluten-free listings do not include a dedicated, celiac-reviewed entry for haishop cafe, so the app's 'options' GF claim has no independent celiac support.
The cafe's GF reputation traces only to a non-celiac lifestyle blog roundup of 'healthy sweets' cafes, which does not assess gluten-free ingredient sourcing or cross-contamination.
Roughly 80% of the food and drink menu is vegan, including a soy-meat vegan burger, a vegan tartare bagel sandwich, and all-vegan soft-serve ice cream.
Ingredients are selected with attention to environment, sourcing, and social impact as part of the cafe's core concept.

name: 博多もつ鍋 前田屋 新宿東口店 (Hakata Motsunabe Maedaya Shinjuku Higashiguc)

claims.text: The Maedaya motsunabe product's declared allergens (wheat, soy, beef, pork, sesame) and the traditional wheat-based chanpon-noodle finish mean the dish as normally served is not gluten-free; no dedicated gluten-free process was found.
The broth is a soy-sauce/miso base, and the brand's own allergen labeling for this motsunabe includes wheat and soy, indicating standard (wheat-containing) soy sauce and miso are used.

The menu is built entirely around beef and pork offal hot pot with a meat-based broth; no vegetable or plant-based broth alternative was found in any source, so the kitchen does not appear set up for vegan dining.
